claims.source: We found that this phenotype worsens after P14 (Figure 1J–L).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental observations shown in Figure 1J-L.

claims.claim: GluN1 KO mice showed no differences with littermate controls at P0, P3, and P5.
claims.source: GluN1 KO mice showed no differences with littermate controls at P0, P3, and P5 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1) indicating no difference in the overall rate of axon growth.
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental observations shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: GluN1 KO mice showed earlier and increased innervation of S1 at P6, when callosal axons start entering the contralateral cortex.
claims.source: However, GluN1 KO mice showed earlier and increased innervation of S1 at P6, when callosal axons start entering the contralateral cortex (Figure 2B and E).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental observations shown in Figure 2B and E.

claims.claim: In control littermates at P6, callosal axons were gathered into a bundle under contralateral S1 with few axons penetrating into S1.
claims.source: In control littermates, at P6, callosal axons were gathered into a bundle under contralateral S1 with few axons penetrating into S1.
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental observation shown in Figure 2A.

claims.claim: In GluN1 KO mice at P6, axons targeting S1 had extended past layer V, with many axons terminating in layer II/III.
claims.source: In contrast, axons targeting S1 in GluN1 KO mice at P6 had extended past layer V, with many axons terminating in layer II/III (arrows in S1 in Figure 2B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental observation shown in Figure 2B.

claims.claim: Control mice showed equal degrees of callosal innervation from medial to lateral S1 at P6.
claims.source: Interestingly, while control mice showed equal degrees of callosal innervation from medial to lateral S1 (see arrows in S1 in Figure 2A), GluN1 KO mice showed preferential early callosal innervation of medial S1 (see arrows in S1 in Figure 2B), and this was even more apparent at P8 (Figure 2C and D).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental observations shown in Figure 2A.

claims.claim: GluN1 KO mice showed preferential early callosal innervation of medial S1 at P6.
claims.source: Interestingly, while control mice showed equal degrees of callosal innervation from medial to lateral S1 (see arrows in S1 in Figure 2A), GluN1 KO mice showed preferential early callosal innervation of medial S1 (see arrows in S1 in Figure 2B), and this was even more apparent at P8 (Figure 2C and D).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental observations shown in Figure 2B.

claims.claim: In control mice, cleaved caspase-3+ cells were mostly detected in layer II/III of primary motor cortex (M1), and rarely were observed in other cortical regions.
claims.source: In control mice, cleaved caspase-3+ cells were mostly detected in layer II/III of primary motor cortex (M1), and rarely were observed in other cortical regions (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A).
claims.evidence: This is supported by cleaved caspase-3 immunostaining shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2A.

claims.claim: GluN1 KO mutants had increased cell death in layer II/III of M1.
claims.source: Mutants did have increased cell death in layer II/III of M1 (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B'); however, there was no increase in cell death in other cortical regions including S1 (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B'').
claims.evidence: This is supported by cleaved caspase-3 immunostaining shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2B'.

claims.claim: There was no increase in cell death in S1 of GluN1 KO mutants.
claims.source: Mutants did have increased cell death in layer II/III of M1 (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B'); however, there was no increase in cell death in other cortical regions including S1 (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B'').
claims.evidence: This is supported by cleaved caspase-3 immunostaining shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2B''.

claims.claim: The deletion of NMDAR in excitatory cortical neurons leads to premature and disrupted callosal innervation of contralateral S1.
claims.source: Taken together, these data indicate that the deletion of NMDAR in excitatory cortical neurons leads to premature and disrupted callosal innervation of contralateral S1.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data showing earlier and increased callosal innervation in NMDAR mutants.

claims.claim: The excessive callosal innervation in NMDAR mutants persists and is not corrected by pruning of mistargeted axons at later developmental stages.
claims.source: Furthermore, this excessive innervation persists and is not corrected by pruning of mistargeted axons at later developmental stages.
claims.evidence: This is based on observations that the phenotype continues to worsen after P14.

claims.claim: Presynaptic deletion of GluN1 from neurons had no discernible effect on callosal innervation at P14.
claims.source: Compared with littermate controls (Figure 3B), presynaptic deletion of GluN1 (ipsiS1-/-) from neurons had no discernible effect on callosal innervation at P14 (Figure 3C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental observations shown in Figure 3B and 3C.

claims.claim: NMDAR is not required for projecting neurons to properly target S1.
claims.source: This suggests that NMDAR is not required for projecting neurons to properly target S1.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that presynaptic deletion of GluN1 had no effect on callosal innervation.

claims.claim: Selective deletion of postsynaptic GluN1 strikingly increased callosal S1 innervation.
claims.source: However, selective deletion of postsynaptic GluN1 in experimental mice strikingly increased callosal S1 innervation (Figure 3G and H, Figure 3—figure supplement 1) similar to the deletion of GluN1 in all excitatory cortical neurons (Figure 1G).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental observations shown in Figure 3G, 3H, and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: NMDAR is required in the target neurons only for normal callosal circuit formation.
claims.source: These results suggest that NMDAR is required in the target neurons only for normal callosal circuit formation.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that postsynaptic but not presynaptic deletion of GluN1 disrupts callosal innervation.

claims.claim: Anti-NMDAR antibodies directed to an extracellular domain of GluN1 downregulate the numbers of surface NMDARs.
claims.source: NMDAR antibodies directed to an extracellular domain of GluN1 are known to downregulate the numbers of surface NMDARs.
claims.evidence: This is based on established knowledge about the effects of anti-NMDAR antibodies.

claims.claim: The anti-GluN1 antibody can alter the surface distribution and dynamics of NMDAR.
claims.source: It has been shown that this antibody can alter the surface distribution and dynamics of NMDAR (Dupuis et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claims.claim: The distribution of anti-GluN1 antibodies was most abundant in deep cortical layers of the ipsilateral injected hemisphere.
claims.source: The distribution of anti-GluN1 antibodies was most abundant in deep cortical layers of the ipsilateral injected hemisphere (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental observation shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: Contralateral but not ipsilateral antibody injections led to more overall callosal innervation in S1 at P14.
claims.source: The fluorescence density analysis at P14 showed that the contralateral (Figure 4E–H) but not ipsilateral antibody injections (Figure 4A–D) led to more overall callosal innervation in S1 at P14.
claims.evidence: This is supported by fluorescence density analysis shown in Figure 4.

claims.claim: Contralateral/target expression of NMDAR in deep cortical layers is required for callosal axon targeting.
claims.source: This further supports our genetic data that contralateral/target expression of NMDAR in deep cortical layers is required for callosal axon targeting.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the antibody injection experiments showing that contralateral but not ipsilateral injections affect callosal innervation.

claims.claim: Antibody injections from P4 to P8 had increased callosal axonal growth into S1 similar to that observed in NMDAR genetic deletion mice.
claims.source: We found that antibody injections from P4 to P8 had increased callosal axonal growth into S1 similar to that observed in NMDAR genetic deletion mice (Figure 5A–D).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental observations shown in Figure 5A-D.

claims.claim: Antibody injections only from P8 to P14 had no effect on the overall callosal innervation pattern.
claims.source: However, antibody injections only from P8 to P14 had no effect on the overall callosal innervation pattern and we saw no increased callosal innervation in S1 (Figure 5E–H).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental observations shown in Figure 5E-H.

claims.claim: The crucial effect of NMDAR on callosal circuit formation is primarily during callosal projection into the cortex (P6–P8).
claims.source: Thus, taking the genetic and antibody injection data together suggests that the crucial effect of NMDAR on callosal circuit formation is primarily during callosal projection into the cortex (P6–P8).
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the temporal specificity of the antibody injection effects.

claims.claim: GluN2A- and GluN2B-containing NMDARs are functionally distinct.
claims.source: GluN2A- and GluN2B-containing NMDARs are functionally distinct (Kutsuwada et al., 1992; Loftis and Janowsky, 2003) and follow different developmental expression trajectories with GluN2B as the major NR2 subunit during the first postnatal week and GluN2A expression present but increasing thereafter (Liu et al., 2004; Monyer et al., 1994; Sans et al., 2000; Sheng et al., 1994).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claims.claim: GluN2B is the major NR2 subunit during the first postnatal week and GluN2A expression is present but increasing thereafter.
claims.source: GluN2A- and GluN2B-containing NMDARs are functionally distinct (Kutsuwada et al., 1992; Loftis and Janowsky, 2003) and follow different developmental expression trajectories with GluN2B as the major NR2 subunit during the first postnatal week and GluN2A expression present but increasing thereafter (Liu et al., 2004; Monyer et al., 1994; Sans et al., 2000; Sheng et al., 1994).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claims.claim: GluN2A was dramatically diminished in Emx1cre/+; Grin2afl/fl mice at P8.
claims.source: To address previous studies that found that GluN2A was expressed at lower levels during development, we checked the expression of GluN2A in S1 at P8 and found that it was dramatically diminished in Emx1cre/+; Grin2afl/fl mice (Figure 6—figure supplement 2A and B), while the expression of GluN2B was the same in control and Emx1cre/+; Grin2afl/fl mice (Figure 6—figure supplement 2A and C), and similarly GluN2A expression was unchanged in Emx1cre/+; Grin2bfl/fl mice (data not shown).
claims.evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2A and B.

claims.claim: The expression of GluN2B was the same in control and Emx1cre/+; Grin2afl/fl mice.
claims.source: To address previous studies that found that GluN2A was expressed at lower levels during development, we checked the expression of GluN2A in S1 at P8 and found that it was dramatically diminished in Emx1cre/+; Grin2afl/fl mice (Figure 6—figure supplement 2A and B), while the expression of GluN2B was the same in control and Emx1cre/+; Grin2afl/fl mice (Figure 6—figure supplement 2A and C), and similarly GluN2A expression was unchanged in Emx1cre/+; Grin2bfl/fl mice (data not shown).
claims.evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2A and C.

claims.claim: In GluN2A KO mice, the overall callosal innervation pattern was similar to control mice, although there was increased callosal innervation at the M1/S1 border at P14.
claims.source: In GluN2A KO mice, the overall callosal innervation pattern was similar to control mice, although there was increased callosal innervation at the M1/S1 border at P14 (Figure 6A–C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental observations shown in Figure 6A-C.

claims.claim: GluN2B deletion phenocopied GluN1 deletion with increased S1 innervation and loss of targeted innervation of the S1/S2 border at P14.
claims.source: In contrast, GluN2B deletion phenocopied GluN1 deletion with increased S1 innervation and loss of targeted innervation of the S1/S2 border at P14 (Figure 6D–F).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental observations shown in Figure 6D-F.

claims.claim: GluN2B KO mice were smaller than littermate controls after P5 and rarely survived past P30.
claims.source: Similar to GluN1 KO mice, GluN2B KO mice were smaller than littermate controls after P5 and rarely survived past P30.
claims.evidence: This is an experimental observation about the phenotype of GluN2B KO mice.

claims.claim: Either GluN2A-containing or GluN2B-containing NMDAR is channel competent.
claims.source: Either GluN2A-containing or GluN2B-containing NMDAR is channel competent and GluN2A-containing NMDARs are present in the cortex of GluN2B KO mice, thus it seems possible that NMDAR's role in callosal circuit development may be separable from its channel activity.
claims.evidence: This is based on established knowledge about NMDAR subunit composition and function.

claims.claim: NMDAR's role in callosal circuit development may be separable from its channel activity.
claims.source: Either GluN2A-containing or GluN2B-containing NMDAR is channel competent and GluN2A-containing NMDARs are present in the cortex of GluN2B KO mice, thus it seems possible that NMDAR's role in callosal circuit development may be separable from its channel activity.
claims.evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the observation that GluN2B deletion causes a phenotype despite the presence of channel-competent GluN2A-containing NMDARs.

claims.claim: Ca2+ influx through NMDARs is essential for synaptogenesis, experience-dependent synaptic remodeling, and long-lasting changes in synaptic efficacy such as LTP and LTD.
claims.source: Ca2+ influx through NMDARs is essential for synaptogenesis, experience-dependent synaptic remodeling, and long-lasting changes in synaptic efficacy such as long-term potentiation (LTP) and long-term depression (LTD) (Collingridge et al., 2004; Lau and Zukin, 2007).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature and represents established knowledge.

claims.claim: There are NMDAR functions independent of its ion-influx.
claims.source: However, accumulating evidence shows that there are NMDAR functions independent of its ion-influx (Kessels et al., 2013; Nabavi et al., 2013), such as a use-dependent tyrosine dephosphorylation of NMDA receptors is independent of ion flux (Vissel et al., 2001), and NMDAR-dependent LTD which can be induced independent of Ca2+ influx (Dore et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claims.claim: In models of ischemic stroke, neuronal death caused by overactivation of NMDAR is independent of Ca2+ influx, but dependent on signaling complexes formed by NMDARs, Src kinase, and Panx1.
claims.source: In models of ischemic stroke, neuronal death caused by overactivation of NMDAR is also independent of Ca2+ influx, but dependent on signaling complexes formed by NMDARs, Src kinase, and Panx1 (Weilinger et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claims.claim: MK-801 is a non-competitive NMDAR antagonist that enters the open NMDAR channel and binds to the 'blocking site' located deep in the pore, blocking Ca2+ influx through NMDAR.
claims.source: MK-801 enters the open NMDAR channel and binds to the 'blocking site' located deep in the pore, blocking Ca2+ influx through NMDAR (Huettner and Bean, 1988, Figure 7A).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature and represents established knowledge about MK-801 mechanism of action.

claims.claim: Blocking NMDAR with a daily dose of 0.4 mg/kg MK-801 in ferret pups between P14 and P21 disrupted axonal pattern formation by retinal afferents in the lateral geniculate nucleus.
claims.source: Previous studies showed that blocking NMDAR with a daily dose of 0.4 mg/kg MK-801 in ferret pups between P14 and P21 disrupted axonal pattern formation by retinal afferents in the lateral geniculate nucleus (LGN) (Hahm et al., 1999).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claims.claim: MK801-treated pups gained weight slowly and developed opisthotonic posturing of limbs and head, suggesting the channel function of NMDAR had been blocked.
claims.source: Compared with saline control, MK801-treated pups gained weight slowly and developed opisthotonic posturing of limbs and head (data not shown), suggesting the channel function of NMDAR had been blocked.
claims.evidence: This is an experimental observation and inference about the effectiveness of MK-801 treatment.

claims.claim: The normal callosal innervation pattern in MK-801 treated pups was similar to saline-treated controls.
claims.source: However, the normal callosal innervation pattern in these pups was similar to saline-treated controls (Figure 7B–D).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental observations shown in Figure 7B-D.

claims.claim: D-APV competitively blocks the ligand (glutamate) binding site to NMDAR and inhibits channel opening, thereby preventing Ca2+ influx.
claims.source: We also performed similar experiments using D(-)−2-amino-5-phosphonopentanoic acid (D-APV), which competitively blocks the ligand (glutamate) binding site to NMDAR and inhibits channel opening, thereby preventing Ca2+ influx (Morris, 1989, Figure 7E).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature and represents established knowledge about D-APV mechanism of action.

claims.claim: D-APV-treated pups developed unilateral muscle contractions in limbs on the opposite side of the injection, suggesting the channel function of NMDAR had been blocked.
claims.source: Compared with saline control, D-APV-treated pups developed unilateral muscle contractions in limbs on the opposite side of the injection (data not shown), suggesting the channel function of NMDAR had been blocked.
claims.evidence: This is an experimental observation and inference about the effectiveness of D-APV treatment.

claims.claim: The callosal innervation pattern in D-APV treated pups was similar to saline controls.
claims.source: However, the callosal innervation pattern in these pups was again similar to saline controls (Figure 7F–H).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental observations shown in Figure 7F-H.

claims.claim: NMDAR function in callosal targeting is independent of its channel activity.
claims.source: Taken together, these results indicate that NMDAR function in callosal targeting is independent of its channel activity.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that blocking NMDAR channel activity with MK-801 or D-APV does not affect callosal innervation patterns.

claims.claim: NMDAR subunits bind directly to EPHB axon guidance receptors.
claims.source: Previous studies have shown that NMDAR subunits bind directly to EPHB axon guidance receptors (Dalva et al., 2000).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claims.claim: EPHB receptor tyrosine kinases and their transmembrane-ligands, the EPHRIN-B family, mediate short-distance cell–cell signaling and regulate many developmental processes including ordered neural maps.
claims.source: EPHB receptor tyrosine kinases and their transmembrane-ligands, the EPHRIN-B family, mediate short-distance cell–cell signaling and thus regulate many developmental processes at the interface between pattern formation and morphogenesis, including ordered neural maps (Kania and Klein, 2016; Niethamer and Bush, 2019).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature and represents established knowledge.

claims.claim: EPHRIN-B1 and EPHB2 are involved in earlier stages of CC midline axon crossing.
claims.source: Further, several members of the EPH/EPHRIN family, including EPHRIN-B1 and EPHB2, are involved in earlier stages of CC midline axon crossing, strengthening their relevance in this context (Bush and Soriano, 2009; Orioli et al., 1996; Robichaux et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claims.claim: EPHB2 and NMDARs colocalize at postsynaptic dendrites.
claims.source: EPHB2 and NMDARs colocalize at postsynaptic dendrites, and the extracellular domain of NMDAR interacts directly with EPHB2, an interaction driven by activation of EPHB2 by clustered EPHRIN-B1 expressed in presynaptic axon terminals (Dalva et al., 2000; Nolt et al., 2011; Palmer and Klein, 2003).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claims.claim: The extracellular domain of NMDAR interacts directly with EPHB2, an interaction driven by activation of EPHB2 by clustered EPHRIN-B1 expressed in presynaptic axon terminals.
claims.source: EPHB2 and NMDARs colocalize at postsynaptic dendrites, and the extracellular domain of NMDAR interacts directly with EPHB2, an interaction driven by activation of EPHB2 by clustered EPHRIN-B1 expressed in presynaptic axon terminals (Dalva et al., 2000; Nolt et al., 2011; Palmer and Klein, 2003).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claims.claim: Mice lacking EPHB2 have reduced levels of NMDARs at synapses in the hippocampus and cortex.
claims.source: Mice lacking EPHB2 have reduced levels of NMDARs at synapses in the hippocampus and cortex (Henkemeyer et al., 2003; Sheffler-Collins and Dalva, 2012), suggesting coordinated localization.
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claims.claim: EPHB2 preferentially decreases Ca2+-dependent inactivation of GluN2B-containing NMDARs but not GluN2A-containing NMDARs at synapses of mature neurons.
claims.source: EPHB2 also preferentially decreases Ca2+-dependent inactivation of GluN2B-containing NMDARs but not GluN2A-containing NMDARs at synapses of mature neurons (Nolt et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claims.claim: EPHB2 signaling leads to phosphorylation of GluN2B at tyrosine residue 1472 preventing clathrin-dependent endocytosis, and increasing the surface retention of GluN2B-containing NMDARs.
claims.source: In addition, EPHB2 signaling leads to phosphorylation of GluN2B at tyrosine residue 1472 preventing clathrin-dependent endocytosis, and increasing the surface retention of GluN2B-containing NMDARs (Chen and Roche, 2007; Nolt et al., 2011; Takasu et al., 2002).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claims.claim: At P5, EPHB2 was found in both cortex and CC of controls.
claims.source: At P5, EPHB2 was found in both cortex and CC of controls (Figure 8—figure supplement 1A).
claims.evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1A.

claims.claim: In GluN1 KO mice, EPHB2 expression in the cortex was reduced.
claims.source: However, in GluN1 KO mice, EPHB2 expression in the cortex was reduced (Figure 8—figure supplement 1B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1B.

claims.claim: Protein levels of EPHB2 were reduced at least 30% in GluN1 KO mice.
claims.source: Western blots also confirmed that protein levels of EPHB2 were reduced at least 30% in GluN1 KO mice (Figure 8—figure supplement 1C–E) while mRNA levels of EPHB2 were unchanged (Figure 8—figure supplement 1F).
claims.evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1C-E.

claims.claim: mRNA levels of EPHB2 were unchanged in GluN1 KO mice.
claims.source: Western blots also confirmed that protein levels of EPHB2 were reduced at least 30% in GluN1 KO mice (Figure 8—figure supplement 1C–E) while mRNA levels of EPHB2 were unchanged (Figure 8—figure supplement 1F).
claims.evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1F.

claims.claim: The punctate staining of EPHB2 on cell membranes was completely lost in red (recombined) cells of Emx1cre/+; Grin1fl/fl; Rosa26fs-tdTomato brain sections.
claims.source: Supporting our hypothesis that loss of GluN1 leads to loss of EPHB2, the punctate staining of EPHB2 on cell membranes was completely lost in red (recombined) cells of Emx1cre/+; Grin1fl/fl; Rosa26fs-tdTomato brain sections but not red cells of Emx1cre/+; Grin1wt/wt; Rosa26fs-tdTomato brain sections (Figure 8—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: Loss of NMDAR caused the loss of EPHB2 selectively on cells that lack GluN1 after excision.
claims.source: Taken together, we demonstrated that the loss of NMDAR caused the loss of EPHB2 selectively on cells that lack GluN1 after excision, thus explaining the 30% reduction in EPHB2 protein expression.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the immunostaining data showing loss of EPHB2 in GluN1-deleted cells.

claims.claim: When NMDARs are lost, membrane based EPHB2 protein expression in target neurons is lost as well.
claims.source: Because EPHB2 is necessary for localization of NMDAR to postsynaptic terminals, we wondered if this requirement was reciprocal and found indeed that it is – when NMDARs are lost, membrane based EPHB2 protein expression in target neurons is lost as well (Figure 8—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: NMDAR reciprocally regulates the localization of EPHB2.
claims.source: This result suggests that NMDAR reciprocally regulates the localization of EPHB2.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that loss of NMDAR leads to loss of EPHB2.

claims.claim: In projecting neurons lacking EPHRIN-B1, callosal axons extended into the cortex past layer V, and many axons terminated in layer II/III, similar to that observed in GluN1 KO mice at P6.
claims.source: In projecting neurons lacking EPHRIN-B1, callosal axons extended into the cortex past layer V, and many axons terminated in layer II/III (arrows in Figure 8C), similar to that observed in GluN1 KO mice at P6 (Figure 2B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental observations shown in Figure 8C.

claims.claim: Unclustered soluble EPHRINs bind EPH receptors but act as antagonists.
claims.source: EPHRINs have to be clustered in a cell membrane or artificially with, for example, antibodies to efficiently activate EPH receptors (Davis et al., 1994). Unclustered soluble EPHRINs bind EPH receptors but act as antagonists (Vearing and Lackmann, 2005).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature and represents established knowledge.

claims.claim: Contralateral injection of soluble EPHRIN-B1-Fc led to increased callosal innervation at P6 with axons penetrating to superficial layers.
claims.source: Compared with littermate controls, contralateral injection of soluble EPHRIN-B1-Fc led to increased callosal innervation at P6 with axons penetrating to superficial layers (Figure 8F, G, and J).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental observations shown in Figure 8F, G, and J.

claims.claim: EPHRIN-B1-EPHB2 play important roles in controlling callosal axon penetration into the contralateral S1 cortex.
claims.source: These results support the idea that EPHRIN-B1-EPHB2 play important roles in controlling callosal axon penetration into the contralateral S1 cortex.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental results showing that blocking EPHRIN-B1-EPHB2 signaling increases callosal innervation.

claims.claim: Contralateral injection of anti-GluN1 antibodies caused increased callosal innervation at P6 and penetration to superficial layers of cortex.
claims.source: Compared with controls, contralateral injection of anti-GluN1 antibodies caused increased callosal innervation at P6 and penetration to superficial layers of cortex (Figure 8D, E, and J).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental observations shown in Figure 8D, E, and J.

claims.claim: Blocking NMDAR and EPHRIN-B1-EPHB2 signaling simultaneously in contralateral cortex did not show any additive or synergistic effects.
claims.source: Critically, blocking NMDAR and EPHRIN-B1-EPHB2 signaling simultaneously in contralateral cortex by injecting both anti-GluN1 antibody and EPHRIN-B1-Fc did not show any additive or synergistic effects (Figure 8H–J).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental observations shown in Figure 8H-J.

claims.claim: NMDAR and EPHRIN-B1-EPHB2 are in the same pathway in regulating callosal targeting in S1.
claims.source: This suggests that in fact NMDAR and EPHRIN-B1-EPHB2 are in the same pathway in regulating callosal targeting in S1 and is consistent with our other findings.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that blocking both systems simultaneously is not additive.

claims.claim: NMDARs cooperate with EPHRIN-B/EPHB in controlling callosal circuit formation.
claims.source: In this study, we found that NMDARs cooperate with EPHRIN-B/EPHB in controlling callosal circuit formation and demonstrated that it is GluN2B-containing NMDARs in target S1 cortex that regulate callosal axon targeting in S1.
claims.evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the experimental findings.

claims.claim: In mutants where either GluN2B or GluN1 are disrupted, there is excess axonal growth throughout S1.
claims.source: In mutants where either GluN2B or GluN1 are disrupted, there is excess axonal growth throughout S1.
claims.evidence: This is a summary of the experimental findings.

claims.claim: This phenotype is most consistent with a loss of a repellant activity that normally restricts commissural axonal projections to the S1 cortex at initial stages of this process.
claims.source: We believe this phenotype is most consistent with a loss of a repellant activity that normally restricts commissural axonal projections to the S1 cortex at initial stages of this process (Figure 2).
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental findings.

claims.claim: The complementary expression of Sema3A and Nrp1 contributes to axonal order within the CC.
claims.source: The complementary expression of chemotropic guidance cue Semaphorin3A (Sem3A) and its receptor Neuropilin-1 (Nrp1) contributes to this axonal order within the CC.
claims.evidence: This is based on previous work by the authors.

claims.claim: Sema3A/Nrp1 signaling contributes to the topographic order of axons within the CC but is not involved in the axon position-dependent projection to the contralateral target cortex.
claims.source: The studies of genetic manipulations showed that Sema3A/Nrp1 signaling contributes to the topographic order of axons within the CC but is not involved in the axon position-dependent projection to the contralateral target cortex.
claims.evidence: This is based on previous work by the authors.

claims.claim: Contralateral/target expression of NMDAR controls the pattern of callosal projections to contralateral target S1.
claims.source: Here, in this study, we demonstrated that contralateral/target expression of NMDAR controls the pattern of callosal projections to contralateral target S1.
claims.evidence: This is a summary of the experimental findings.

claims.claim: Despite the disruption of targeting within S1 in mice with disrupted NMDAR, there is little evidence of ectopic projection to other cortical areas.
claims.source: Interestingly, despite the disruption of targeting within S1 in mice with disrupted NMDAR, there is little evidence of ectopic projection to other cortical areas.
claims.evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data.

claims.claim: There are other cues that regulate the generic projection to S1 but the mechanisms uncovered help govern the distribution of these axons within S1.

claims.source: This is consistent with a role for NMDAR in controlling initial projection into S1 but probably also later regulating refinement of these inappropriate projections by pruning – both core functions of axonal repellants.

results.result: Normal postnatal development of S1 callosal projections follows a stereotyped pattern: axons reach white matter under contralateral S1 by P5, are diffusely distributed at P8, refine to a narrow S1/S2 border band by P12, and remain stable thereafter.
results.evaluation: Claims C23-C26 describe a consistent developmental trajectory supported by experimental observations in Figures 1B-E. The temporal progression and anatomical specificity are clearly documented with appropriate imaging evidence.

results.result: GluN1 knockout mice show disrupted callosal innervation patterns with uniform distribution throughout S1 rather than selective S1/S2 border targeting, and significantly increased overall callosal axon density at P14.
results.evaluation: Claims C2-C3, C28, C33-C36 collectively demonstrate the primary phenotype with both qualitative imaging (Figures 1F-G) and quantitative analysis (Figures 1H-I). Statistical significance is reported (p-values provided) and the phenotype is reproducible across multiple animals.

results.result: The callosal innervation defect in GluN1 KO mice worsens progressively after P14, with nearly sixfold increased axonal extension into S1 by P30 when animals die.
results.evaluation: Claims C37-C38, C4, and C125 document progressive worsening of the phenotype with quantitative support (Figures 1J-L). The temporal progression and magnitude of change are clearly documented, though the mechanism of progressive worsening is not explained.

results.result: GluN1 KO mice show premature callosal innervation of S1 starting at P6, with axons extending past layer V into layer II/III and preferential early innervation of medial S1, while showing no differences at P0, P3, or P5.
results.evaluation: Claims C39-C44 and C48 establish the critical developmental window when the phenotype first appears. The data show normal development until P6, then premature and aberrant innervation patterns (Figures 2A-E, Figure 2—figure supplement 1). This temporal specificity is well-documented.

results.result: GluN1 KO mutants show increased cell death in layer II/III of motor cortex (M1) but not in S1 or other cortical regions at P6.
results.evaluation: Claims C45-C47 address whether increased cell death could explain the mis-innervation phenotype. Cleaved caspase-3 staining (Figure 2—figure supplement 2) shows region-specific cell death that does not correlate with the callosal innervation defect, ruling out this alternative explanation.

results.result: NMDAR is required specifically in postsynaptic target neurons but not in presynaptic projecting neurons for normal callosal circuit formation, as demonstrated by selective deletion experiments.
results.evaluation: Claims C50-C53 establish the critical cellular localization of NMDAR function through complementary experiments (Figures 3A-H). Presynaptic deletion has no effect while postsynaptic deletion phenocopies the global knockout, providing strong evidence for target-specific requirements.

results.result: Contralateral but not ipsilateral injection of anti-GluN1 antibodies into the lateral ventricle from P2-P12 increases callosal innervation in S1 at P14, confirming that target expression of NMDAR in deep cortical layers is required for callosal axon targeting.
results.evaluation: Claims C54-C58 use antibody-mediated loss of function to confirm the genetic results. The spatial specificity (contralateral vs ipsilateral) and antibody distribution data (Figure 4—figure supplement 1) support the conclusion, though antibody penetration and efficacy could be better characterized.

results.result: The critical period for NMDAR function in callosal circuit formation is during P4-P8 when axons project into cortex, as antibody injections during P4-P8 but not P8-P14 disrupt callosal innervation.
results.evaluation: Claims C59-C61 define the temporal window of NMDAR requirement through time-restricted antibody injections (Figure 5). The differential effects of early vs late injections clearly establish P6-P8 as the critical period, consistent with the genetic data showing phenotype onset at P6.

results.result: GluN2B but not GluN2A deletion phenocopies GluN1 deletion with disrupted callosal innervation, despite both subunits being expressed at P8 and both forming channel-competent receptors.
results.evaluation: Claims C62-C68 establish subunit-specific requirements through knockout comparisons (Figure 6). Western blot confirms expression levels (Figure 6—figure supplement 2), and the differential phenotypes are clear. However, sample sizes for GluN2B KO are small (n=2 at P14), which weakens statistical confidence.

results.result: NMDAR's role in callosal circuit development may be separable from its channel activity, as GluN2B deletion causes a phenotype despite the presence of channel-competent GluN2A-containing NMDARs.
results.evaluation: Claims C69-C70 present a speculative interpretation. While the logic is reasonable (GluN2A receptors are present and channel-competent in GluN2B KO mice), this inference alone is insufficient without direct testing of channel-independent functions. The subsequent pharmacological experiments (C74-C81) provide stronger support.

results.result: NMDAR function in callosal targeting is independent of its ion channel activity, as blocking Ca2+ influx with MK-801 or D-APV does not affect callosal innervation patterns despite causing behavioral changes indicating effective channel blockade.
results.evaluation: Claims C74-C81 provide strong evidence for channel-independent function through pharmacological blockade (Figure 7). Both MK-801 and D-APV show no effect on callosal innervation despite clear systemic effects. However, the dosing rationale could be better justified, and local drug concentrations in target tissue are not measured.

results.result: Loss of NMDAR causes loss of EPHB2 protein (30% reduction) selectively on cells lacking GluN1, with unchanged mRNA levels, demonstrating that NMDAR reciprocally regulates EPHB2 localization.
results.evaluation: Claims C90-C97 establish reciprocal regulation through multiple approaches: immunostaining, western blot, and cell-specific analysis using Cre-reporter mice (Figure 8—figure supplements 1-2). The combination of population-level and single-cell data is compelling, though the 30% reduction is modest and mechanistic details are lacking.

results.result: NMDAR and EPHRIN-B1-EPHB2 act in the same pathway to control callosal axon targeting, as deletion of EPHRIN-B1 in projecting neurons or blocking EPHB with EPHRIN-B1-Fc phenocopies NMDAR loss, and simultaneous blockade of both systems is not additive.
results.evaluation: Claims C98, C100-C104, C119, C121-C122 demonstrate pathway convergence through genetic and pharmacological epistasis experiments (Figure 8). The lack of additivity when blocking both systems simultaneously (Figure 8H-J) is strong evidence for a common pathway, though the EPHRIN-B1 deletion phenotype is less severe, possibly due to redundancy.

results.result: NMDARs cooperate with EPHRIN-B/EPHB in target cortex to regulate callosal circuit formation, likely by acting as a repellant to limit early growth of callosal axons into S1 cortex.
results.evaluation: Claims C105, C7, C8, and C124 synthesize the major findings into a mechanistic model. The repellant model is well-supported by the premature and excessive innervation phenotype, the postsynaptic requirement, and the EPHRIN-B/EPHB interaction. However, direct demonstration of repulsive activity is lacking.

results.result: Blocking Ca2+ influx through NMDAR with MK-801 or D-APV causes subtle, local laminar-specific innervation differences at the S1/S2 border, suggesting that refinement of axon arborization may rely on Ca2+ influx-mediated activity changes.
results.evaluation: Claims C130-C131 describe subtle effects not shown in figures and use speculative language ('may rely'). Without quantification or visual documentation of these 'subtle differences,' this result cannot be properly evaluated. This appears to be an observation that requires further investigation.

results.result: GluN1 expression is greatly diminished in GluN1 KO mice at P8, while thalamocortical barrel organization in Layer IV of S1 is somewhat disrupted but still apparent.
results.evaluation: Claims C31-C32 validate the knockout model and address potential confounds. Western blot and immunostaining (Figure 1—figure supplement 1) confirm GluN1 deletion, while VGlut2 staining shows preserved barrel structure, indicating the callosal phenotype is not secondary to complete loss of cortical organization.

results.result: NMDAR plays a role in both controlling initial projection into S1 and later regulating refinement of inappropriate projections by pruning, consistent with a loss of repellant activity that normally restricts commissural axonal projections.
results.evaluation: Claims C126, C49, and C107 interpret the progressive worsening of the phenotype as evidence for dual roles in initial targeting and subsequent pruning. The interpretation is reasonable given the data, though direct evidence for impaired pruning (e.g., time-lapse imaging) is not provided.
